body.text: It’s a long way from Funafuti to Havana, but Tuvalu has joined other developing countries in supporting Cuba as the Caribbean nation endures an expanding US blockade.

At the UN General Assembly in September, the Pacific island state’s prime minister, Feleti Teo, said his nation “remains troubled by the longstanding unilateral economic measures imposed on Cuba.” His call for the sanctions to be lifted was echoed by other Pacific leaders during the UN’s annual opening session.

“For thirty-three consecutive years, this Assembly has called for an end to the embargo against Cuba,” said president David Adeang of Naoero (formerly Nauru). “Naoero reiterates that call, and we encourage dialogue grounded in full respect for sovereignty.”

Vanuatu’s permanent UN representative Odo Tevi stressed that “the imposition of coercive economic measures, including unilateral sanctions, against developing countries is unfair and unjust… In this respect, we consistently call for the uplift of the economic embargo on the Republic of Cuba.”

This show of solidarity reflects growing ties between Pacific nations and a socialist country they once scorned as a Russian proxy. Cuba now trains hundreds of Pacific medical students, sends medical workers around the region and collaborates with Pacific nations as a member of the Alliance of Small Island States, or AOSIS, and the UN Special Committee on Decolonisation.

Havana’s call for South–South solidarity is escalating, however, as Cuba faces an energy and humanitarian crisis under deepened sanctions and a fuel blockade imposed by Donald Trump. Despite the looming dominance of the Democrats in the US Congress following voters’ massive midterm rebuke, Trump continues to muse about foreign interventions during his two remaining years in office.

“I wanna get Cuba done before I leave,” he said on 12 November. “Frankly, I’d love to be able to do it for the people, for the Cubans that came and were treated really badly, and they came to America.”

US secretary of state Marco Rubio, the son of Cuban exiles, is also fixated on toppling the Cuban government. The Florida politician, who once claimed his parents fled Fidel Castro’s 1959 revolution — in fact they left Cuba in 1956 during Fulgencio Batista’s military dictatorship — has long promoted hawkish policies to undermine the government in Havana. Now, with Trump’s support, he might finally be unleashed.
“We have a very good, talented guy for Cuba named Marco,” Trump said. “Because Marco Rubio, his parents are from Cuba, as you probably know, and he would love to do that.”

Relations between the US and Cuba thawed under Barack Obama, who visited Havana in March 2016. But Trump put Cuba back on the US list of state sponsors of terrorism during his first presidency, and since his re-election in 2024 he has reiterated criticism of Cuba’s human rights record and placed renewed emphasis on security in the Western hemisphere. His administration’s 2025 National Security Strategy resolved to “deny non-Hemispheric competitors the ability to position forces or other threatening capabilities, or to own or control strategically vital assets, in our hemisphere.”

Trump’s so-called “Donroe Doctrine” echoes the 1823 declaration by president James Monroe that the Western Hemisphere was off-limits to European interference. Monroe argued that any actions in Latin America by European powers would be viewed as a hostile threat to American security. Fast forward two centuries and the policy is now directed against China.

But the real challenge to US power is local, not external. Since 2024, electoral victories by progressive candidates in Mexico, Uruguay and now Brazil have challenged Trump’s vision of US hegemony. In response, his administration has ramped up pressure on the left-wing governments in Venezuela and Cuba, seen as sources of “ideological infection” in Central and South America.

In January this year, Trump’s Operation Absolute Resolve seized Venezuelan president Nicolás Maduro. Trump then imposed an oil blockade on Cuba, damaging the island’s electrical grid and triggering a humanitarian crisis. He also signed an executive order declaring Cuba an “unusual and extraordinary threat” to the United States and banned all oil exports to Cuba from Venezuela.

As well, the US has reinforced longstanding extraterritorial measures against companies that trade or invest in Cuba, introducing secondary sanctions against businesses, banks and other suppliers that operate in Cuba, backed by the threat of extra tariffs on any country that supplies Cuba with fuel.

In May, Trump raised the possibility of US military intervention in Cuba, and last month Rubio called on people who “seek to create positive change in Cuba” to “seize this opportunity to create the change you desire through a discrete [sic] partnership with the CIA.”

In a report to the United Nations last July, UN Special Rapporteur on unilateral coercive measures Alena Douhan noted that “the overarching unilateral coercive measures imposed on Cubans and the overcompliance by various actors have a devastating effect on the entire population, especially persons living in poverty, women, children, older persons, persons with disabilities and persons with chronic diseases.”

Speaking at the UN General Assembly in September, Cuba’s foreign minister Bruno Rodríguez Parrilla claimed that infant mortality has doubled under the US blockade, and “70 per cent of the Essential Medicines List is lacking. Around 100,000 persons, of them more than 12,000 children, are awaiting surgery.”

Last month, the UN General Assembly considered its annual resolution calling for an end to the US’s sixty-four-year-old economic restrictions on Cuba. The resolution passed with 130 in favour, seventeen against and twenty-five abstentions. In a worrying sign for the government in Havana, however, the vote showed a decline in support compared with similar resolutions in recent years. In 2024, the vote was 187–2 with only the United States and Israel opposed. Last year, the vote was 165 in favour with seven opposing.

The US has been pressuring Caribbean and Latin American states to break ties with Cuba. Last month, US ambassador to the United Nations Mike Waltz condemned corruption and political repression in Havana, declaring: “History is watching. Vote no on this resolution. Stand with the Cuban people.”
As US and Cuban diplomats shoved each other and shouted insults on the floor of the General Assembly, Cuba’s UN ambassador Ernesto Soberón Guzmán launched a scathing attack on his US counterpart.

“Mr Waltz, since you have taken to acting like an inquisitive little elephant, I must ask: why is Cuba unable to import fuel freely, as any other nation can?” Soberón asked. “Why are threats of tariffs, as well as secondary and extraterritorial sanctions, levelled against anyone who dares to engage in commercial activity with our country? You must finally come to understand, you imperialists, that Cuba is neither a colonial possession of the United States nor a defeated enemy.”

In response to the US blockade, Cuba has been looking for greater support from other nations, including the small island developing states that make up 20 per cent of the UN membership. In 2013 the Pacific Islands Forum granted Cuba “dialogue partner” status alongside major powers like the United States, China, France and Japan. (An application for partnership status from Spain, Cuba’s former colonial power, was deferred that year, due to anger over Spain’s role in aggressive EU fishing operations in Pacific waters.)

At the following year’s Forum, Cuba’s non-resident ambassador to the Pacific Islands, María del Carmen Herrera Caseiro, presented her credentials. In 2017, Cuba established an embassy in Suva, currently headed by ambassador Néstor Torres Olivera.

“As a small island with limited resources, we must join forces with similar countries that face similar challenges like climate change,” Torres told me. “We must also act on what is happening now in the world, in the Middle East, which also affects the small countries. We’re very proud that we have graduated in Cuba over 240 students from the Pacific Islands, and they are serving now in their countries, working very hard in their communities, in those poor areas.”

Those doctors and medical officers were trained in primary and preventative health at Escuela Latinoamericana de Medicina, or ELAM, an international public medical university in Havana. Another large group of almost 1000 ELAM trainees are East Timorese.

Despite the economic crisis facing Cuba under the US blockade, the annual offer of medical scholarships for young Pacific Islanders remains in place. “Our scholarships are for poor people who want to become a doctor, and we give them that chance to go to Cuba to pursue that dream,” said Torres. “While our main focus in the Pacific Islands is South–South cooperation, specifically in the health system, we also try to promote and market products from the Cuban biotechnology.”

Since the opening of the embassy in Suva, Torres has held discussions with Forum Island health officials to promote Cuban-developed drugs like Neuralcim (a medication that can slow the progression of Alzheimer’s disease) and Heberprot-P (an injection that accelerates deep tissue healing to treat severe diabetic foot ulcers and prevent amputations).

Torres said the embassy in Suva was also holding talks with Fiji Sugar Corporation on potential research collaboration, exchange of technical knowledge, and the use of sugarcane byproducts. Another sector for collaboration is high-performance sports coaching in areas of common competitive strength like weightlifting and boxing.
But this collaboration is hampered by the current fuel crisis in Cuba, and the looming threat of intervention from the United States.

“For the last seven months, there has not entered one single oil tanker to the country, can you imagine that?” Torres said. “The island has blackouts that last for over forty, fifty hours. The hospitals are not running in the full capacity. There are thousands of people waiting for surgery, because not all the hospitals have a generator. Food production is another big issue in the country, because of lack of transportation to the factories.”

The US mid-term elections saw a stunning rebuff to Donald Trump and the MAGA movement. But with two years remaining in office, Trump retains control of most foreign affairs powers. Launching the war on Iran, he was willing to ignore the US Congress and its constitutional role in endorsing new military operations. Cuba remains in the firing line and is looking to other small island states to take up the call for an end to blockade and sanctions. •
